title: Babur Offers His Life for His Son
text:
In 1530 Humayun, the eldest son of Babur, founder of the Mughal empire, fell gravely ill. He was brought to Agra, and the doctors could do nothing for him. His sister Gulbadan Begum, who was a child at the time, later wrote the story in her memoir of her brother's reign, the Humayun-nama.

According to her account, those around the emperor suggested that he give away something of great value, in the hope that God would accept it in exchange for his son's life. Babur answered that nothing he owned was as valuable as his own life, and that he would give that. He walked three times around Humayun's bed, praying that the illness pass from his son to himself.

Gulbadan writes that from that day Humayun began to recover, while Babur himself fell ill. His condition worsened over the following months. He gathered his nobles, named Humayun as his successor, and asked them to be loyal to him. Babur died at Agra in December 1530, at forty-seven.

Humayun's reign proved difficult. He lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri and spent fifteen years in exile, but he reconquered Delhi shortly before his death, and his son Akbar became the greatest of the Mughals.
lesson: Many parents would take a child's suffering upon themselves if they could. That love is real even when it cannot change what happens.
source: Gulbadan Begum, Humayun-nama (Ahval-i Humayun Badshah), trans. Annette Beveridge (1902)
caveat: The account comes from Babur's daughter, writing decades later; historians note Babur may already have been in poor health.
